passage.title: The Solar Car
paras: The science fair was only three days away, and Turki’s solar car still would not move. He had attached the small solar panel and the motor, but when he put the car in the sunlight, the wheels stayed still.
“Maybe it just does not work,” Turki said, dropping into a chair in his grandfather’s workshop. He felt frustrated and tired.

His grandfather, who had repaired radios for forty years, picked up the car and turned it over slowly. “A machine is like a story,” he said. “If one part is missing, the whole thing stops. Let us look for the missing part.”
Together they checked every wire. At last, Turki noticed that one wire from the panel was not touching the motor. He fixed it, carried the car outside, and watched the wheels begin to spin.

“You see?” said his grandfather. “You did not need a new car. You needed patience.” On the day of the fair, Turki’s car crossed the whole hall, and he explained to the judges how he had found the problem.

passage.title: The Night Market Stall
paras: On Thursday nights, Talal helped his father sell spices at the night market. He measured cumin and cardamom into small bags and wrote the prices on cards.

One night, a customer pushed a bag back across the table. “This saffron is too expensive,” he said loudly. “The man at the next stall sells it for less.” Talal felt his face get hot. He wanted to argue.

His father spoke first. “You are right to compare,” he said calmly. He opened two small jars and let the man smell both. “This one is from last year. This one arrived yesterday. Choose the one you prefer.”

The man smelled the fresh saffron, paused and then smiled. He bought the more expensive bag. When he had gone, Talal asked, “Why did you not argue with him?” His father replied, “An argument wins a moment. Respect wins a customer.”

passage.title: The Arabian Oryx and the Fennec Fox
paras: Both the Arabian oryx and the fennec fox live in hot deserts, but they have adapted to their habitat in different ways.
**The Arabian Oryx**

The Arabian oryx is a large white antelope with long, straight horns. Its white coat reflects sunlight and helps keep it cool. The oryx can go for weeks without drinking, because it gets water from plants and dew. By 1972, it had disappeared from the wild, but careful protection programs brought it back, and today wild herds live in protected areas again.
**The Fennec Fox**

The fennec fox is the smallest fox in the world. Its huge ears help heat leave its body. It is **nocturnal**, so it sleeps in a cool burrow during the day and hunts insects and small animals at night.
**Two Ways to Survive**
The oryx is large and active in the early morning and evening, whereas the fennec fox is tiny and active at night. Yet both animals conserve water and avoid the hottest part of the day.

passage.title: The Dhow and the Container Ship
paras: For centuries, traders in the Arabian Gulf and the Red Sea sailed wooden boats called **dhows**. Today, giant container ships carry most of the world’s goods. The two kinds of ships are very different, but they share the same purpose: moving goods across the sea.
A dhow is made of wood and pushed by the wind in its large triangular sails. It usually has a small crew and can carry dates, spices, cloth and fish. Its journeys depend on the seasonal winds.

A container ship is made of steel and powered by huge engines. It can be longer than three football fields and carry thousands of metal boxes called containers. Because it does not need the wind, it can sail at any time of year.
Although container ships carry far more, dhows have not disappeared. Builders still make them by hand in some coastal towns, and many are used for fishing and for short trips.

passage.title: Students Need More Time to Read
paras: Our school should add twenty minutes of free reading to every school day. Reading every day is one of the best ways to become a stronger student.
First, daily reading builds vocabulary. Students who read often meet thousands of new words each year, and they learn them in context.
Second, reading helps students concentrate. In a short survey of our Grade 5 class, most students said that they felt calmer after reading quietly.
Third, reading is enjoyable. When students choose their own books, they want to read more, and the more they read, the better they become.
**Our Class Survey: How do you feel after 20 minutes of reading?** — Calmer: 14 students · The same: 6 students · Less calm: 2 students
Some people say there is no time in the school day. However, twenty minutes is only a small part of a seven-hour day, and the benefits are large. I recommend that we start next week.

paras: **Text 1: Grandmother’s Garden (a story)**

Every summer, Nawaf visited his grandmother’s farm in Al-Ahsa. Early in the morning, she showed him how the water ran through narrow channels to each palm tree. “My father dug these channels,” she said. “Now they are yours to look after.” Nawaf pressed his hand into the cool, wet soil and felt proud.
**Text 2: The Oasis of Al-Ahsa (an article)**

Al-Ahsa, in eastern Saudi Arabia, is one of the largest oases in the world. Water from underground springs has supported farming there for thousands of years. Farmers built irrigation channels to carry the water to millions of date palms. In 2018, UNESCO added the Al-Ahsa Oasis to its World Heritage List because of its long history of people living with nature.

Before dawn, Jaber watched his father tie a stone to his foot and dive from the boat. Jaber counted slowly: one, two, three… Each time his father came up, he opened his hand to show a few oysters. Most held nothing. “The sea gives slowly,” his father said, breathing hard. “But the sea is fair.”

Before oil was discovered, pearl diving was one of the most important industries in the Arabian Gulf. Divers used stones to sink quickly to the seabed and held their breath for about a minute or more while they collected oysters. A diver might open hundreds of oysters to find one valuable pearl. In the 1930s, cheaper cultured pearls from Japan reduced the demand for natural pearls, and the industry declined.

passage.title: The Kite Festival
paras: Mazen had spent two weeks building a kite shaped like a falcon. On the morning of the kite festival, the wind was perfect, and hundreds of colourful kites filled the sky over the beach.
Mazen’s little cousin, Rakan, stood beside him with a broken plastic kite. Its tail had snapped, and it kept spinning into the sand. Rakan’s lip trembled, but he did not cry.
Mazen looked at his falcon, then at Rakan. He knelt down, tore a strip of cloth from his own kite’s long tail, and tied it to Rakan’s kite. “Try now,” he said.

Rakan’s kite climbed into the air and stayed there. Mazen’s falcon flew a little lower than before, but it did not matter. The judges did not give Mazen a prize that day, yet when Rakan shouted, “Look, it is flying!”, Mazen felt as if he had won the biggest one.

passage.title: Ibn Battuta: The Great Traveller
paras: In 1325, a young man named Ibn Battuta left his home in Tangier, Morocco, to perform Hajj in Makkah. He was twenty-one years old. He did not know that his journey would last almost thirty years.
After Hajj, Ibn Battuta kept travelling. He visited Egypt, Syria, Persia and East Africa. He crossed Central Asia and worked as a judge in India. Later he sailed to China.

When he finally returned to Morocco, the Sultan asked him to tell the story of his travels. A writer named Ibn Juzayy wrote down his words. The book, often called the *Rihla* (“The Journey”), describes the cities, people and customs he saw.
Today historians use the *Rihla* to learn about life in the fourteenth century. Ibn Battuta travelled about 120,000 kilometres, farther than almost any other traveller of his time.

passage.title: The Rose Harvest of Taif

passage.title: The Tortoise in the Courtyard
paras: One morning, Hamza found a small desert tortoise in his grandfather’s courtyard. Its shell was the color of sand, and it blinked at him slowly, as if it were deciding whether he could be trusted.

“It is trying to go home,” said Grandfather quietly. Hamza’s throat felt tight. “But I take good care of it,” he said.

paras: More than 800 years ago, an engineer named Ismail al-Jazari worked in the city of Diyarbakir. He designed clever machines that moved by themselves using water, weights and gears.

In 1206, he finished a famous book that described about fifty of his machines. For each one, he drew careful pictures and wrote clear instructions so that others could build it. His designs included water pumps, locks and clocks.
His best-known invention is the **Elephant Clock**. A bowl that slowly filled with water and sank inside the elephant measured the time. Every half hour, figures moved and a cymbal sounded.

passage.title: Two Calendars
paras: Most countries use the **Gregorian calendar**, which follows the Sun. A year in this calendar is 365 days long, or 366 days in a leap year.

Muslims also use the **Hijri calendar**, which follows the Moon. It begins with the Hijrah, when the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) moved from Makkah to Madinah in the year 622 CE. Each month begins when the new crescent moon is seen.
Like the Gregorian calendar, the Hijri calendar has twelve months. However, a lunar year has only about 354 days, so it is about eleven days shorter than a solar year.

Because of this difference, Hijri months move earlier through the seasons every year. Ramadan, for example, can fall in summer for some years and in winter years later. In Saudi Arabia, both calendars are used in daily life.
